Photoredox-Catalyzed 1,4-Peroxidation−Sulfonylation of Enynones:
AThree-ComponentRadicalCouplingApproachfortheSynthesisof
Highly Functionalized Allenes
Divya Bhatt, Kosei Miyake, Shuichi Nakamura,* Hun Young Kim,* and Kyungsoo Oh*
Cite This:Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 2955−2959
 Read Online
ACCESS

ABSTRACT: An Eosin Y-catalyzed visible light-promoted 1,4-
peroxidation−sulfonylation of enynones was achieved to give
tetrasubstituted allenes. The photoredox catalysis of Eosin Y allowed
theconcomitant formationof peroxyandsulfonylradicals, wherethe
preferentialperoxy radical additionto the alkenemoiety of enynones
resulted in the subsequent α-keto radical−sulfonyl radical cross
couplings.ThedevelopedphotoredoxcatalysisofEosinYdemonstratesaregioselective1,4-diradicaladditionstrategy,openingupa
new possibility of diradical functionalization of conjugate systems.
G
iven the widespread synthetic utility of cumulenes,1 the
synthesis of functionalized allenes such as allenols2 and
allenones3 has attracted considerable interest from the
synthetic community. As one of the direct allenylation
strategies,4 the transition metal-catalyzed addition reactions
to 1,3-enynes provide the metalated allenyl intermediates that
lead to the related allenyl products under thermodynamic
control (Scheme 1a). The metalated allenyl intermediate was
first utilized by the Lu’s group to give CN-substituted allenes
under the visible light-induced dual Ir-photoredox/Cu-
catalyzed 1,4-carbocyanation of 1,3-enynes (Scheme 1b).
5
The use of cyclobutanone oxime esters as alkyl radical
precursors was explored by the Guo’s group under similar
dualIr-photoredox/Cu-catalyzed conditionsto givethe highly
functionalized allenes.
6 The regioselective 1,4-arylsulfonyla-
tions of 1,3-enynes were independently developed by the
groups of Li,7 Wang,8 and Lu9 under the dual catalysis of
photoredox and nickel, where sulfinate salts and aryl halides
wereusedascouplingpartners.In2022,theKong’sgroupalso
disclosed the combination of photo-hydrogen atom transfer
catalyst, decatungstate, and nickel catalysis for the 1,4-
dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to give tetrasubstituted
CF
3-allenes.10 Morerecently,theWang’sgroupdevelopedthe
dual 4-CzIPN photoredox and chromium catalysis for the
asymmetric 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to the chiral
allenols.
11 In contrast to the previous dual metal/photoredox
catalysis approaches, the Zhang’s group explored the dual Ir-
photoredox/NHC-catalyzed 1,4-sulfonylacylation of 1,3-
enynes using sodium sulfinate salts and aroyl fluorides.12
Suchanonmetal-based1,4-hydroxysulfonylationof1,3-enynes
was also explored by the Wu’s group under the Ir-photoredox
catalysis using water and sulfonyl chlorides.
13 Inspired by the
recent advances in the visible light-promoted photoredox
sulfonylation14 as well as the metal-catalyzed radical perox-

15
we became interested in a visible light photoredox
catalysis for the 1,4-peroxidation/sulfonylation of 1,3-enynes
(Scheme 1c). Our group recently reported the chemodivergent
sulfonylation of enynones, where the sulfonyl radical addition
occurred at the alkene moiety of enynones.
16
Nevertheless, the
prediction of the reaction pathways of two different radical
species, peroxy and sulfonyl, was deemed to be challenging
because of the persistent character of peroxy and sulfonyl
radical species. Herein, we report the visible light photoredox
catalysis of Eosin Y for the diradical functionalization of
enynones, ensuring the chemoselective peroxy radical addition,
followed by a consequent addition of the sulfonyl radical to
enynones. The developed visible light photoredox diradical
1,4-functionalization of 1,3-enynes provides highly function-
alized allene derivatives via the sequential installation of two
different radical species in a three-component coupling
strategy.
The photoredox-catalyzed 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes was explored using enynone 1a, p-toluenesulfinic acid
2a, and t-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP in 70 wt.% in H
2
O) in
CH
3
CN under visible light LEDs (Table 1). The use of Ir- and
Ru-based photoredox catalysts led to the formation of desired
allene 3a as a diastereomeric mixture in 8−15% yields (entries
1 and 2). The screening of organo-photocatalysts revealed that
the formation of 3a could be improved to 29−44% yields upon
using Rose Bengal (entry 4), Mes-AcrBF
4
(entry 5), Na
2

Y (entry 7), and Eosin Y (entry 8). The subsequent solvent
screening under Eosin Y catalysis did not fare well (entries 9−
14), only a mixed solvent of DCE:H
2
O showed a marginally
comparable outcome to the 37% yield of 3a (entry 10). The
increased catalyst loading of Eosin Y did little to improve the
reaction efficiency (entry 15). Eventually, the significantly
improved yield of 3a was achieved upon increasing the TBHP
content to 6 equiv (entry 17), where the product 3a was
isolated in 68% yield. The optimal use of 3 mol % Eosin Y
photocatalyst was needed (entry 18). The subsequent variation
of visible light source confirmed the necessity of green LED’s
for the Eosin Y photocatalysis (entries 19−21). The control
experiments in the absence of Eosin Y photocatalyst (entry 22)
or visible light (entry 23) confirmed the critical needs of visible
light LED’s and Eosin Y photocatalyst for the formation of 3a.
The reaction under air instead of an argon atmosphere
negatively influenced the formation of 3a in 15% yield,
suggesting the decomposition pathways of the involved radical
species under an oxygen atmosphere (entry 24). The use of a
nonaqueous solution of TBHP in decane also provided the
desired product 3a in 64% yield (entry 25), a slightly lower
yield than the TBHP in water (entry 17).
With the optimized visible light Eosin Y catalysis for the 1,4-
peroxidation−sulfonylation of enynone, the substrate scope
was investigated using various enynones 1 and sulfinic acids 2
(Scheme 2). The electronic and steric effects of the ketone
moiety (R
1
) of enynones 1 were investigated using phenyl
groups with electron-donating (3b) and electron-withdrawing
groups (3c and 3d), as well as cyclohexyl (3e) and 2-furanyl
(3f) groups, where the desired tetrasubstituted allenes were
obtained as 1:1−1:1.8 diastereomeric mixtures in 37−63%
yields. The R
2
substituent of the alkyne moiety in enynones 1
tolerated alkyl (3g), alkyl chloride (3h), ester (3i), and N-
phthaloyl (3j) groups to give the desired products in 32−60%
yields. The R
3
substituent of the alkene moiety in enynones 1
could accommodate the electronically diverse phenyl and
heteroaryl groups to give tetrasubstituted allenes 3k−3o in
36−59% yields. The radical coupling partner, sulfinic acid 2,
could also tolerate electronically diverse phenyl sulfinic (3p−
3r) and aliphatic sulfinic groups (3s and 3t).
To better understand the current visible light photocatalysis
of Eosin Y, the 1,4-peroxidation−sulfonylation of enynones 1a
was performed in the presence of radical inhibitors (Scheme
3). The desired product 3a was not observed upon adding 2
equiv of TEMPO, only leading to the formation of the sulfinic
acid addition product 4a in an ionic mode.
16
However, the
HRMS analysis of the crude reaction mixture confirmed the
detection of TEMPO-Ot-Bu 4b and TEMPO-captured allenic
or propargyl adducts 4c, suggesting the possible generation of
the t-butoxy radical and propargyl radical species. While the
use of another radical capture reagent, butylated hydroxyto-
luene (BHT), failed to intercept the radical species, 1,1-
diphenylethylene provided the corresponding sulfonyl- and t-
butyl peroxy radical-captured products 4d and 4e in 12−16%
yields. The hydrogen atom of sulfinic acid 2 turned out to be
critical, since the sodium sulfinate 2a-Na, instead of sulfinic
acid 2a, led to the exclusive formation of the alkynyl epoxide
5a and 5b in 54−61% yields. In such an epoxidation pathway,

each reaction component, sodium sulfinate 2a-Na, TBHP,
Eosin Y photocatalyst, and green LEDs, played important roles
in the reaction; thus, the omission of any component led to no
reaction. The employment of chalcone, instead of 1a, also
provided sulfonyl addition product 6a and t-butyl peroxy
addition product 6b in 28% and 19% yields, respectively. The
radical clock experiment confirmed the radical addition to the
alkene moiety, where the adjacent cyclopropyl ring was opened
and the preferential sulfonyl addition product 6c was obtained
in 14% yield. The fluorescence quenching experiments
indicated that the excited state of Eosin Y was quenched by
THBP,
18b
while the sulfinic acid 2a could not quench the
Eosin Y (see the Supporting Information for details). The light
on/off experiment suggested the necessity of continued visible
light irradiation for meaningful reaction progress. The peroxide
moiety in the allene 3a could be manipulated to give the
allenol 7 in 52% yield under the AgOTf catalysis. Alternatively,
the ketone moiety of 3a could be selectively reduced to the
corresponding alcohol 8 in 63% yield using CeCl
3
−NaBH
4
reduction conditions, whereas the concomitant cyclization to
the product 9 was observed in 51% yield using NaBH
4
alone.
Upon heating in o-xylene, the disproportionation of 3a was
observed to give the 2-alkylidene-1,3-diketone 10 in 32% yield
along with 4-nitrobenzaldehyde as a byproduct.
Based on the control experiments, a plausible reaction
mechanism of the photoredox catalysis of Eosin Y for 1,4-
peroxidation−sulfonylation of enynones is proposed in Scheme
4. With the maximum absorption of Eosin Y around 530 nm,
17
the application of green LED’s generates the photoexcited state
of [Eosin Y]* that subsequently undergoes a single electron
transfer to TBHP to give a t-butoxy radical and a hydroxyl
anion.
18
The subsequent hydrogen abstraction by the hydroxyl
anion from the sulfinic acid 2 (pK
a
= 7.1; TBHP pK
a
= 12.8) is
believed to be critical since the use of sodium sulfinate 2a-Na
led to the epoxidation pathway of enynones 1. The resulting
sulfinate anion A should undergo a single electron transfer to
the Eosin Y radical cation [Eosin]
•+
to give the sulfonyl radical
B with the regeneration of the photocatalyst Eosin Y. The fate
of the t-butoxy radical is governed by the ample presence of
TBHP, where the formation of the t-butyl peroxy radical and t-
BuOH should be encouraged.
19
A ready availability of the t-

butyl peroxy radical species initiates the radical addition to the
alkene moiety of enynones 1, where the resulting α-keto radical
species C can be stabilized by the adjacent carbonyl and
alkynyl groups.
4
The final radical−radical coupling between
the sulfonyl radical B and the α-keto radical C occurs at the γ-
carbon of enynones 1 with less steric effect to give the allene
product 3. In the absence of the sulfinic acid 2 the Eosin Y-
promoted photolytical formation of hydroxyl anion acts as a
base to deprotonate TBHP. The resulting t-butyl peroxide
anion should behave as nucleophile adding to the enynones 1
to provide the epoxide product 5 via the intermediate D.
20
It
should be noted that while the previous photoredox-catalyzed
reactions utilized TBHP as oxidants,
18a,b,21
the current results
demonstrated the first peroxidation reaction involving TBHP
under the photoredox catalysis.
In summary, we developed a visible light photoredox
catalysis system for the 1,4-difunctionalization of enynones
using a readily available organophotocatalyst, Eosin Y. The
regioselective two different radical addition strategies were
made possible by using TBHP and sulfinic acids, where the
preferential t-butyl peroxy radical addition to the alkene moiety
of enynones followed by the resulting α-keto radical-sulfonyl
radical cross-coupling was achieved. With ready access to
highly functionalized tetrasubstituted allenes, the developed
visible light photoredox catalysis of Eosin Y should be
applicable to the difunctionalization of other conjugated
systems, 1,n-enynes, using two different radical species. Our
current efforts are directed to such radical difunctionalization
strategies, and these results will be subject of future
publications.
